subject: Quantitative Aptitude
topic: Prime Numbers — properties, identification, word problems

questions.stem: Which of the following is a prime number?
questions.explanation: 23: only divisible by 1 and itself. Trap: picking odd but not prime.

questions.stem: How many prime numbers are there between 1 and 20?
Which is the smallest odd prime number?
questions.explanation: 2 is smallest prime, but even. Smallest odd prime = 3. Trap: picking 1 (not prime).

questions.stem: What is the sum of first 3 prime numbers?
questions.explanation: First 3 primes: 2,3,5. Sum=10. Trap: including 1 or skipping 2.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a prime number?
questions.explanation: 15: divisible by 3,5. Trap: picking odd as prime.

questions.stem: What is the next prime after 19?
questions.explanation: Next prime after 19 is 23. Trap: picking next odd.

questions.stem: If p is a prime number greater than 2, which of the following is always even?

options.option_text: p×p

questions.explanation: All primes >2 are odd, so odd+1=even. Trap: picking p×p (odd×odd=odd).

questions.stem: Which of the following is a pair of twin primes?

options.option_text: 3 and 7, which differ by 4 (not a twin prime pair)
11 and 13, consecutive primes differing by exactly 2
5 and 9, where 9 = 3² is a composite, not a prime
17 and 21, where 21 = 3 × 7 is a composite number

questions.explanation: Twin primes are pairs of primes differing by exactly 2. (11, 13): both prime, 13 − 11 = 2 ✓. (3, 7) differ by 4, not 2. (5, 9): 9 = 3² is composite. (17, 21): 21 = 3 × 7 is composite. The most tempting wrong answer is (3, 7) because both are prime, but candidates forget that twin primes must differ by exactly 2.

questions.stem: Every prime number greater than 3 must be expressible in which of the following forms?

options.option_text: Of the form 4k + 1 for some positive integer k
Of the form 6k ± 1 for some positive integer k
Of the form 4k + 3 for some positive integer k
Of the form 8k ± 1 for some positive integer k

questions.explanation: Any prime p > 3 is not divisible by 2 or 3, so p mod 6 must be 1 or 5, i.e., p = 6k + 1 or 6k − 1 (written 6k ± 1). Verify: 5 = 6×1−1, 7 = 6×1+1, 11 = 6×2−1, 13 = 6×2+1. The form 4k+1 fails for p = 7 (= 4×1+3). The form 8k±1 fails for p = 11 (= 8×1+3, not ±1).

questions.stem: A natural number N has exactly three distinct factors. Which of the following best describes N?

options.option_text: The square of a prime number (e.g., 4, 9, 25, or 49)
The product of two distinct primes p and q, i.e., p × q
A perfect cube of a prime number, such as 8, 27, or 125
A prime number itself, possessing only 1 and itself as factors

questions.explanation: If N = p² (p prime), its only factors are 1, p, and p² — exactly three. The product p × q (distinct primes) has four factors: 1, p, q, pq. A prime cube p³ also has four factors: 1, p, p², p³. A prime has only two factors. The most tempting distractor is p × q because candidates confuse 'product of primes' with 'few factors'.

questions.stem: How many prime numbers lie strictly between 50 and 100?

options.option_text: 8 prime numbers exist in the open interval (50, 100)
10 prime numbers exist in the open interval (50, 100)
12 prime numbers exist in the open interval (50, 100)
9 prime numbers exist in the open interval (50, 100)

questions.explanation: Primes between 50 and 100 (exclusive): 53, 59, 61, 67, 71, 73, 79, 83, 89, 97 — exactly 10. Common errors: 51 = 3×17, 57 = 3×19, 77 = 7×11, and 91 = 7×13 are composite. Candidates who include 91 (mistaking it for prime) or 57 count 12; those who also miss 53 land on 9.

questions.stem: The product of two prime numbers is 437. What is their sum?

options.option_text: 38, obtained by summing the two prime factors of 437
42, obtained by summing the two prime factors of 437
40, obtained by summing the two prime factors of 437
44, obtained by summing the two prime factors of 437

questions.explanation: Test prime divisors: 437 ÷ 19 = 23 exactly, so 437 = 19 × 23 (both prime). Sum = 19 + 23 = 42. The trap option 40 lures candidates who incorrectly try 17 × 23 = 391 ≠ 437. The option 38 = 17 + 21 involves 21, which is not prime. Self-verify: 19 × 23 = (20−1)(20+3) = 400 + 60 − 20 − 3 = 437 ✓.

questions.stem: How many prime numbers p, where p < 20, have the property that p² + 2 is also prime?

options.option_text: No prime p below 20 makes p² + 2 a prime number at all
Exactly one prime (p = 3) satisfies this; 3² + 2 = 11 is prime
Exactly two primes (p = 3 and p = 5) satisfy this condition
Exactly three primes (p = 3, 5 and 7) satisfy this condition

questions.explanation: Check each prime < 20: p=2 → 4+2=6 (composite); p=3 → 9+2=11 ✓ prime; p=5 → 25+2=27=3³ (composite); p=7 → 49+2=51=3×17; p=11 → 123=3×41; p=13 → 171=9×19; p=17 → 291=3×97; p=19 → 363=3×121. The pattern: for any odd prime p ≠ 3, p ≡ 1 or 2 (mod 3) ⟹ p² ≡ 1 (mod 3) ⟹ p²+2 ≡ 0 (mod 3), i.e., always divisible by 3. Only p = 3 escapes this constraint.

questions.stem: p and q are prime numbers satisfying p² − q² = 72. How many ordered pairs (p, q) exist?

options.option_text: Exactly one ordered pair (p, q) satisfies this equation
Exactly two ordered pairs (p, q) satisfy this equation
Exactly three ordered pairs (p, q) satisfy this equation
Exactly four ordered pairs (p, q) satisfy this equation

questions.explanation: Factorise: (p+q)(p−q) = 72. Both odd primes ⟹ p+q = 2a, p−q = 2b, so 4ab = 72 ⟹ ab = 18. Factor pairs (a > b > 0): (18,1) → p=19, q=17 ✓ both prime; (9,2) → p=11, q=7 ✓ both prime; (6,3) → p=9 (not prime) ✗. Case q=2: p²=76, not a perfect square ✗. Valid pairs: (19,17) and (11,7). Verify: 361−289=72 ✓ and 121−49=72 ✓. Candidates often stop after finding one solution, choosing option A.
